title: Faith accepts revealed things by the word — but the word itself by innate notes
source_text: XXXII. Praeterea istud argumentum supponit nihil nos per fidem amplecti, nisi quod probari potest divino quodam verbo atque testimonio: quod, licet prima fronte videatur esse verissimum atque indubitatum, undiquaque tamen verum non est. Etenim fides nostra aliter accipit res in verbo Dei revelatas, & aliter ipsum Dei verbum, seu divinam revelationem. Siquidem res ipsas a Deo revelatas credimus & suscipimus propter divinam revelationem, & quoniam Deus illis in verbo suo testimonium perhibet. At de ipso Dei verbo, seu divina revelatione alia ratio est. Nam una pars verbi divini potest quidem alteri testimonium perhibere, & una revelatio suscipi propter aliam revelationem qua nobis confirmetur; Verum hic dari non potest progressus in infinitum: Sed tandem sistendum est in aliquo Dei verbo, quod fides nostra propter se suscipiat, & quod authoritatem suam non mutuetur ab aliquo alio extra se Dei verbo, cujus testimonio de eo certi reddamur. Itaque necesse est esse aliquod Dei verbum quod per se nobis innotescat, id est, ex signis & notis insitis, aliisque argumentis atque incitamentis, quibus mens nostra a Spiritu sancto illuminata moveatur ut credat revera tale verbum divinum esse, & ad Deum suam referre originem. Quamvis ergo non sit aliud Dei verbum, quod Scripturae divinitati testimonium perhibeat, nihilominus Scriptura erit legitimum fidei nostrae objectum, si quidem fides est assensus quo verbum Dei amplectimur, & propter illud quaecunque testimonio illius confirmantur. Nec effugere possunt adversarii quin fides eorum tandem resolvatur in aliquod Dei verbum cui fidem adhibeant inducti tantum argumentis & motivis quibusdam, non vero propter aliud verbum Dei, cujus testimonio sanciatur ejus authoritas.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover that argument assumes that we embrace nothing by faith except what can be proved by some divine word and testimony: which, though at first sight it may seem most true and undoubted, yet is not true in every respect. For our faith otherwise accepts the things revealed in the word of God, and otherwise the word of God itself, or divine revelation. Inasmuch as we believe and receive the things themselves revealed by God on account of divine revelation, and because God bears testimony to them in his word. But concerning the word of God itself, or divine revelation, there is another account. For one part of the divine word can indeed bear testimony to another, and one revelation be received on account of another revelation by which it is confirmed for us; But here a progress to infinity cannot be given: But at last a stand must be made in some word of God, which our faith receives for its own sake, and which does not borrow its authority from some other word of God outside itself, by whose testimony we are made certain of it. Therefore it is necessary that there be some word of God which becomes known to us through itself, that is, from implanted signs and notes, and other arguments and incentives, by which our mind illuminated by the Holy Spirit is moved to believe that such a word truly is divine, and refers its origin to God. Although therefore there be no other word of God which bears testimony to the divinity of Scripture, nevertheless Scripture will be a legitimate object of our faith, if indeed faith is the assent by which we embrace the word of God, and on account of it whatever things are confirmed by its testimony. Nor can the adversaries escape but that their faith at last is resolved into some word of God to which they give faith induced only by certain arguments and motives, not indeed on account of another word of God by whose testimony its authority is sanctioned.
pass_b_english: The objection assumes faith accepts only what another divine word proves — true for revealed things, not for the word itself.
Things revealed are believed because God testifies in his word; the word itself cannot be propped by infinite regress of further words.
Faith must finally rest in a word received for its own sake, made known by implanted signs and notes under the Spirit's light.
Scripture needs no second word to witness its divinity — it is still faith's proper object.
Rome's own faith likewise bottoms out in some word accepted by motives, not by yet another divine word.
